title: Communication Basics
description: The building blocks of every radio link: modulation, the spectrum, decibels, tuned circuits and RF filters.

study.title: The communication system
study.body: Every link has a **transmitter** (turns the message into a signal that suits the medium), a **channel** (wire, coax, fiber or free space) and a **receiver** (amplifies, filters and demodulates). The channel attenuates the signal and **noise** is added along the way, mostly in the channel and the receiver front end; the signal-to-noise ratio measures how well the message survives. A link is **simplex** (one way: broadcasting), **half duplex** (both ways, one at a time: walkie-talkie) or **full duplex** (both ways at once: telephone).

study.title: Baseband, modulation and multiplexing
study.body: The message itself (audio, video, data) is the **baseband** signal. It can travel directly on a cable, but not by radio: an efficient antenna is about $\lambda/4$ long, kilometres for audio frequencies. So the message **modulates** a high-frequency carrier by varying its amplitude (AM), frequency (FM) or phase (PM). Modulation also enables **multiplexing**: many signals share one medium on different carriers (FDM), in turns (TDM) or with different codes (CDMA).

study.title: The radio spectrum and bandwidth
study.body:
Radio bands are named per decade, with edges at $3 \times 10^n$ Hz:
- VLF 3–30 kHz, LF 30–300 kHz, MF 0.3–3 MHz (AM broadcast)
- **HF 3–30 MHz** (shortwave), **VHF 30–300 MHz** (FM broadcast 88–108 MHz)
- **UHF 300 MHz–3 GHz** (mobile phones, 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, GPS), SHF 3–30 GHz, EHF 30–300 GHz
A signal occupies a **bandwidth** $BW = f_2 - f_1$ around its carrier, and a band of width $B$ holds $B/\Delta f$ channels of spacing $\Delta f$. A given bandwidth is a smaller fraction of a higher carrier, so wideband services live at VHF and above.

study.title: Decibels and dBm
study.body: Gains and losses are given in dB: $10\log_{10}(P_2/P_1)$, or $20\log_{10}(V_2/V_1)$ when the impedances are equal. In a cascade the dB values simply **add** (losses count negative). Absolute power is given in **dBm**, relative to 1 mW: 0 dBm = 1 mW, 30 dBm = 1 W, −30 dBm = 1 µW, so $P_{out}$ (dBm) = $P_{in}$ (dBm) + gain (dB). Every 3 dB doubles the power, every 10 dB multiplies it by 10.

study.title: Explore: Q and selectivity
study.body: An LC circuit resonates where $X_L = X_C$. Its **Q** is the coil reactance divided by its series resistance (typically 10–200 for LC circuits) and sets the 3-dB bandwidth $BW = f_r/Q$, with $f_1 \approx f_r - BW/2$ and $f_2 \approx f_r + BW/2$. A narrow bandwidth means good **selectivity**: one station passes and its neighbours are rejected. Drag $Q$ and watch how strongly a signal 200 kHz away from the 10.7 MHz resonance is suppressed.

study.title: Parallel tank circuits
study.body: Receivers and oscillators mostly use a **parallel tank**. At resonance it acts as a large resistance $Z_r = QX_L = L/(CR_W)$ (for $Q \geq 10$), where $R_W$ is the coil's series resistance. The Q of a loaded tank is $Q = R_P/X_L$, where $R_P$ is all resistance across the tank ($Z_r$, load and source in parallel). A resistor across the tank therefore lowers Q and widens the bandwidth, a common way to set the BW.

study.title: Filters for communications
study.body: RF bandpass filters are specified by passband, insertion loss and **shape factor**: the bandwidth at high attenuation divided by the passband width (e.g. −60 dB / −6 dB, or −40 dB / −3 dB). An ideal filter has SF = 1; a lower SF means steeper skirts. **LC** filters (Q 10–200) are tunable; **crystal** filters (Q $10^4$–$10^6$) give very narrow, steep passbands; **ceramic** filters (Q of a few thousand) are cheap 455 kHz and 10.7 MHz IF filters; **SAW** filters work from 10 MHz to 3 GHz with a low SF but 10–35 dB insertion loss.

steps.title: A communication link
steps.body: A **transmitter** puts the message on a signal that suits the medium, the **channel** carries it (and attenuates it), and the **receiver** recovers the message. Noise enters along the way, mainly in the channel and in the first stages of the receiver.

steps.prompt: Match each link to its mode of operation.
steps.explanation: Broadcasting only goes one way (simplex). A walkie-talkie works both ways but only one party transmits at a time (half duplex). In a phone call both talk and listen simultaneously (full duplex), which needs separate frequencies or time slots for the two directions.

steps.title: Why modulate?
steps.body: Audio at a few kHz has a wavelength of tens of kilometres, and an efficient antenna is about a quarter wavelength long. Moving the message onto a high-frequency **carrier** makes antennas practical, and giving every station its own carrier lets many signals share the air (frequency-division multiplexing).

steps.prompt: Find the free-space wavelength of a {{f|Hz}} radio signal.
steps.explanation: $\lambda = c/f = 300/f_{\text{MHz}}$ = 300 / {{fM}} = **{{3e8/f|m}}**. A quarter-wave antenna would be {{3e8/f/4|m}} long.

steps.prompt: Suppose you tried to radiate a {{fa|Hz}} audio tone directly, without a carrier. How long would a quarter-wave antenna be?
steps.explanation: $\lambda = c/f$ = (3×10⁸ m/s) / {{fa|Hz}} = {{3e8/fa|m}}, so $\lambda/4$ = **{{3e8/fa/4|m}}**. Impossible in practice; at a 100 MHz carrier the same antenna is only 75 cm. This is the first reason to modulate.

steps.title: The radio spectrum
steps.body:
The bands are decades with edges at $3 \times 10^n$ Hz:
- LF 30–300 kHz, MF 300 kHz–3 MHz (AM broadcast)
- HF 3–30 MHz (shortwave, reflected by the ionosphere)
- VHF 30–300 MHz (FM broadcast, marine, aviation)
- UHF 300 MHz–3 GHz (mobile phones, Wi-Fi, GPS)
- SHF 3–30 GHz (satellite, radar), EHF 30–300 GHz
In wavelength, HF spans 100 m to 10 m, VHF 10 m to 1 m, UHF 1 m to 10 cm.

steps.prompt: A transmitter operates at {{f|Hz}}. In which band does it lie?
steps.explanation: Band edges are at $3 \times 10^n$ Hz: LF 30–300 kHz, MF 0.3–3 MHz, HF 3–30 MHz, VHF 30–300 MHz, UHF 0.3–3 GHz. Find the decade between two edges that contains {{f|Hz}}; its wavelength is {{3e8/f|m}}.

steps.prompt: The peaks of a radio wave in free space are {{lc}} cm apart. What is its frequency?
steps.explanation: The peak spacing is one wavelength. $f = c/\lambda$ = (3×10⁸ m/s) / {{lam}} m = **{{3e8/lam|Hz}}** (or $f_{\text{MHz}} = 300/\lambda$).

steps.prompt: A {{B|Hz}} wide band starting at {{f1|Hz}} is divided into channels spaced {{df|Hz}} apart. How many channels does it hold?
steps.explanation: $N = B/\Delta f$ = {{B|Hz}} / {{df|Hz}} = **{{B/df||4}}** channels. Halving the channel spacing (narrower modulation) doubles the number of users in the same spectrum.

steps.prompt: Order these services from lowest to highest carrier frequency.
steps.explanation: AM broadcast is in the MF band (about 0.5–1.6 MHz), shortwave in HF (3–30 MHz), FM broadcast in VHF (88–108 MHz), mobile phones and Wi-Fi in UHF (0.7–2.7 GHz) and satellite TV in SHF (around 11–12 GHz).

steps.title: Working in dB
steps.body: Convert to dB once, then add and subtract: output (dBm) = input (dBm) + gains (dB) − losses (dB). Convert back only at the end. Useful anchors: +3 dB = ×2, +10 dB = ×10, 0 dBm = 1 mW.

steps.prompt: A power level is {{Pd}} dBm. Express it in watts.
A transmitter delivers {{P|W}}. Express this in dBm (enter the number of dBm in the dB box).
A receiver input gets {{Pin}} dBm from the antenna. It passes a {{G1}} dB low-noise amplifier, a filter with {{L}} dB insertion loss and a {{G3}} dB IF amplifier.

ask.prompt: What is the total gain of the chain in dB?
What is the output power in dBm (enter it in the dB box)?
What is the output power in watts?

steps.prompt: An RF amplifier with equal input and output impedance raises a {{Vin|V}} signal to {{Vout|V}}. What is its gain in dB?
steps.explanation: Equal impedances, so the power gain in dB follows from the voltage ratio: $20\log_{10}(V_{out}/V_{in})$ = 20 log({{A}}) = **{{20*log10(A)}} dB**. (Using $10\log$ on a voltage ratio would give only half.)

steps.prompt: Three stages have power gains of +{{G1}} dB, −{{L}} dB and +{{G2}} dB. What is the overall power gain as a ratio?
steps.explanation: Add the dB values: {{G1}} − {{L}} + {{G2}} = {{Gt}} dB. Then convert once: $10^{ {{Gt}}/10 }$ = **{{10^(Gt/10)||3}}**. Adding the ratios is wrong (ratios multiply), and dividing by 20 is for voltage ratios.

steps.prompt: A {{P|W}} transmitter feeds its antenna through a coax cable with {{L}} dB loss. How much power reaches the antenna?
Match each level to its power.
steps.explanation: dBm is relative to 1 mW: every 10 dB is a factor 10 and 3 dB a factor 2. So 20 dBm = 100 mW, 30 dBm = 1000 mW = 1 W, −30 dBm = 0.001 mW = 1 µW and −3 dBm = 0.5 mW.

steps.prompt: A receiver with a 50 Ω input sees a signal of {{Vu}} µV rms. What is the signal power in dBm (enter it in the dB box)?
steps.explanation:
$P = V^2/R$ = ({{Vu}} µV)² / 50 Ω = {{P*1e15||3}} fW = {{P*1e15||3}} × 10⁻¹⁵ W.
$P_{dBm} = 10\log_{10}(P/1\ \text{mW})$ = **{{10*log10(P/1e-3)}} dBm**. Typical receiver sensitivities are in this range.

steps.prompt: A tuned circuit has $L$ = {{L|H}} and $C$ = {{C|F}}. Find its resonant frequency.
A tuned circuit resonates at {{fr|Hz}} with $Q$ = {{Q}}.

ask.prompt: How far above $f_r$ is the upper 3-dB frequency $f_2$?
ask.explanation: $BW = f_r/Q$ = {{fr/Q|Hz}}. For $Q \geq 10$ the band is nearly symmetric, so $f_2$ lies $BW/2$ = **{{fr/Q/2|Hz}}** above $f_r$.

steps.prompt: A resonant circuit at {{fr|Hz|4}} has $Q$ = {{Q}}. Which are its 3-dB frequencies?
steps.explanation: $BW = f_r/Q$ = {{B|Hz}}. The 3-dB points lie $BW/2$ = {{B/2|Hz}} on either side: $f_1$ = **{{fr-B/2|Hz|5}}**, $f_2$ = **{{fr+B/2|Hz|5}}**.

steps.prompt: A sweep of a tuned amplifier shows 3-dB frequencies of {{f1|Hz|6}} and {{f2|Hz|6}}. What is the Q of the circuit?
steps.explanation: $BW = f_2 - f_1$ = {{B|Hz}}. The centre is $f_r = \sqrt{f_1f_2} \approx (f_1 + f_2)/2$ = {{fr|Hz|4}}. $Q = f_r/BW$ = **{{sqrt(f1*f2)/B||3}}**.

steps.prompt: A parallel tank of $L$ = {{L|H}} (coil resistance $R_W$ = {{Rw}} Ω) and $C$ = {{C|F}} resonates at {{fr|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the Q of the tank.
Find the impedance of the tank at resonance.
ask.explanation: $X_L$ = {{XL|Ω}}, $Q = X_L/R_W$ = {{Q||3}}. $Z_r = QX_L = L/(CR_W)$ = {{L|H}} / ({{C|F}} × {{Rw}} Ω) = **{{L/(C*Rw)|Ω}}**. A few ohms of coil resistance become tens of kilohms at resonance.

steps.prompt: A receiver's input circuit uses $L$ = 1 µH (Q = 15). Tune it to the station at {{fs|Hz}} by setting $C$.
steps.explanation: Resonance at the station: $C = \frac{1}{(2\pi f)^2L}$ = 1 / ((2π × {{fs|Hz}})² × 1 µH) = **{{Ct|F}}**. Turning the tuning capacitor moves the peak; a smaller C tunes higher.

steps.prompt: A bandpass filter is {{B6|Hz}} wide at −6 dB and {{B60|Hz}} wide at −60 dB. What is its shape factor?
steps.explanation: $SF = BW_{-60\,dB}/BW_{-6\,dB}$ = {{B60|Hz}} / {{B6|Hz}} = **{{SF}}**. The closer to 1, the steeper the skirts.

steps.prompt: Match each filter type to its typical property.
steps.explanation: LC filters are easy to tune but their Q is limited by coil losses. Quartz crystals have enormous Q, ideal for narrow SSB and CW filters. Ceramic resonators are cheaper with Q in the thousands, the standard AM and FM IF filters. SAW filters use acoustic waves on a piezoelectric surface and suit VHF to microwave front ends.

steps.prompt: A filter with a shape factor of 3 is more selective than one with a shape factor of 1.5.
steps.explanation: False. The shape factor is the ratio of the stopband width to the passband width. With SF = 1.5 the response falls from −6 dB to −60 dB over a much narrower range, so it rejects nearby signals better. The ideal is SF = 1.

steps.prompt: A tank circuit must resonate at {{fr|Hz}} with a {{L|H}} coil. Which capacitance is needed?
The {{L|H}} coil of a {{fr|Hz}} tank has a series resistance of {{Rw}} Ω.

ask.prompt: Find the bandwidth of the tank.
Find the impedance of the tank at resonance.

steps.prompt: A {{fr|Hz}} tank has $X_L$ = {{XL}} Ω and coil resistance {{Rw}} Ω. Its bandwidth must be widened to {{Bn|Hz}} with a resistor across the tank. Find that resistor (use $R_P = QX_L$).
steps.explanation:
Now: $Q = X_L/R_W$ = {{Q0||3}}, so $R_P = QX_L$ = {{RP|Ω}}.
Needed: $Q = f_r/BW$ = {{Qn||3}}, so $R_P' = QX_L$ = {{RPn|Ω}}.
$R_{ext} \parallel R_P = R_P'$ gives $R_{ext} = \frac{R_PR_P'}{R_P - R_P'}$ = **{{Rx|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: An antenna delivers {{Vu}} µV rms into a 50 Ω front end: a {{G1}} dB LNA, a SAW filter with {{Ls}} dB loss and a {{G2}} dB amplifier. What is the output power in dBm (enter it in the dB box)?
steps.explanation:
Input power: $P = V^2/R$ = ({{Vu}} µV)²/50 Ω = {{(Vu*1e-6)^2/50*1e15||3}} fW, which is $10\log_{10}(P/1\ \text{mW})$ = {{Pin}} dBm.
Output: {{Pin}} + {{G1}} − {{Ls}} + {{G2}} = **{{Pout}} dBm**.

steps.prompt: A filter has a −6 dB bandwidth of {{B6|Hz}} and a shape factor of {{SF}} (−60 dB / −6 dB). How far from the centre frequency must an interfering signal be to be suppressed by at least 60 dB?
steps.explanation: The −60 dB bandwidth is $SF \times BW_{-6\,dB}$ = {{SF}} × {{B6|Hz}} = {{SF*B6|Hz}}, centred on the filter. Half of it on each side: **{{SF*B6/2|Hz}}** from the centre. With an ideal SF = 1 that would be only {{B6/2|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: Which filter technology is the classic low-cost choice for the 10.7 MHz IF of an FM broadcast receiver?
steps.explanation: Ceramic filters are small, cheap and fixed at the standard 10.7 MHz (FM) and 455 kHz (AM) IFs, with a bandwidth around 150–300 kHz for FM. Crystal filters are for much narrower bandwidths (SSB, CW), LC filters cannot reach the needed Q and steepness cheaply, and RC filters are not used at RF.

steps.prompt: The receiver is meant for {{fM}} MHz. How long is a quarter-wave antenna for this frequency?
steps.explanation: $\lambda = 300/f_{\text{MHz}}$ = 300 / {{fM}} = {{300/fM|m}}, so $\lambda/4$ = **{{75/fM|m}}** (a real antenna is a few percent shorter because of end effects).
